steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on few-shot 3D keypoint detection on meshes using features back-projected from pre-trained 2D foundation models. Explain the motivation and gap, why keypoints matter, what our features and symmetry-aware optimization do, and summarize contributions and results.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Foundation models and the missing 3D counterpart

  - successes for text and 2D images (cite); no prominent 3D methods for local details
  - reasons: diverse 3D representations (meshes, point clouds, volumetric, implicit); little high-quality 3D data
- From classification to segmentation to keypoints
  - recent 2D-foundation-model shape analysis (cite): mainly global tasks, shape classification; segmentation = middle ground (cite)
  - this paper continues: classification -> segmentation -> keypoints, each more localized
- Few-shot keypoint detection on 3D meshes
  - task: few-shot keypoint detection on 3D meshes
  - repeatable keypoints -> rigid/non-rigid matching, tracking, reconstruction, manipulation (cite)
  - needs semantic + geometric understanding; testbed for local shape descriptors (cite) and 3D shape/view consistency (cite)
- Back-projected 2D features
  - natural approach: dense 3D features/descriptors capturing global (semantic) + local (geometric) info
  - prior: axiomatic features or pre-training on 3D datasets (cite); robustness issues, little/undiverse 3D data -> limited accuracy on complex models
  - ours: features from pre-trained 2D vision encoders, no further training
  - first to show back-projected features give local geometry + global semantics
  - robust to rotation and scaling; any surface point, any texture
  - multiple rendered views -> coarse 2D features become dense, continuous 3D descriptors
- Handling symmetries
  - common challenge: symmetries
  - detect all keypoints across symmetries (e.g. different legs of a table), no superfluous detections
  - simple optimization using back-projected features: keypoint distribution on target matches few-shot examples
- Contributions and results
  - (1) formalized feature back-projection, Gaussian geodesic re-weighting for noisy visibility
  - (2) analysis of back-projected features from recent foundation models
  - (3) optimization module matching average keypoint distribution on target
  - KeypointNet: state of the art, over 93% IoU better than best competitor, averaged over evaluation distances
  - ablation: 2D extractors vs axiomatic 3D descriptors, optimization components
  - also state of the art on part segmentation transfer

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Foundation models are used in more and more downstream applications. They generalize strongly to tasks they were not explicitly trained for and show surprising zero- or few-shot capabilities. There are successful approaches for processing text or 2D images, but there are no prominent 3D methods yet that are aimed at local details. The main reasons are that there are many different 3D representations (i.e., meshes, point clouds, volumetric or implicit representations) and that high-quality 3D data is comparably scarce.

Recent works that use 2D foundation models for shape analysis have focused mostly on global tasks like shape classification, or on segmentation, which is a middle ground between global and local analyses. This paper builds on this continuum and goes from classification to segmentation and now to keypoints, where each stage needs a more localized understanding of the geometric details.

Repeatable keypoints make many downstream applications possible, for example rigid and non-rigid shape matching, object tracking, shape reconstruction, and shape manipulation. Also, since keypoint detection is a complex problem that needs both semantic and geometric shape understanding, it has been used before as a useful testbed for exploiting and evaluating different local shape descriptors, and also consistency relations between 3D shapes and their views.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Foundation models are used in more and more downstream applications. They generalize strongly to tasks they were not explicitly trained for and show surprising zero- or few-shot capabilities. There are successful approaches for processing text or 2D images, but there are no prominent 3D methods yet that are aimed at local details. The main reasons are that there are many different 3D representations (i.e., meshes, point clouds, volumetric or implicit representations) and that high-quality 3D data is comparably scarce.

Recent works that use 2D foundation models for shape analysis have focused mostly on global tasks like shape classification, or on segmentation, which is a middle ground between global and local analyses. This paper builds on this continuum and goes from classification to segmentation and now to keypoints, where each stage needs a more localized understanding of the geometric details.

In this work we focus on the task of few-shot keypoint detection on 3D meshes. Repeatable keypoints make many downstream applications possible, for example rigid and non-rigid shape matching, object tracking, shape reconstruction, and shape manipulation. Also, since keypoint detection is a complex problem that needs both semantic and geometric shape understanding, it has been used before as a useful testbed for exploiting and evaluating different local shape descriptors, and also consistency relations between 3D shapes and their views.

A natural approach to keypoint detection is to use dense 3D geometric features or descriptors. Ideally these features should capture both global (semantic) and local (geometric) information at the same time. Previous works here either focus on axiomatic features or pre-train models on 3D datasets. But such methods are limited by robustness issues and by the lack of diversity and amount of 3D training data. So existing approaches usually have limited accuracy on complex 3D models. Instead, we propose to get informative features from powerful pre-trained 2D vision encoders, which can be used directly without more training.

We show for the first time that these back-projected features give a localized understanding of shape geometry and at the same time capture rich global semantic information. We show that the features are robust against rotations and scaling changes, and that they can be computed for any point on the surface of the shape and with any texture type. By putting together information from multiple rendered views around the shape, we show that even coarse 2D features can give dense 3D descriptors that vary continuously on the surface.

Besides the lack of informative features, symmetries are a common challenge in keypoint detection. A good method should detect all keypoints across the different symmetries (e.g., different legs of a table) but avoid superfluous detections. For this we introduce a simple but effective optimization strategy that uses the back-projected features and makes sure the detected keypoints have a similar distribution on the target shapes as on the given few-shot examples.

Our main contributions are (1) formalizing feature back-projection, including Gaussian geodesic re-weighting to handle noisy point visibility information, (2) analyzing back-projected features from different recent foundation models and their properties, and (3) an optimization module that tries to match the average observed distribution of keypoints on the target shape. Our method gets state-of-the-art results on the KeypointNet benchmark and improves over the best competing method by over 93% IoU on average over all evaluation distances. In an extensive ablation study we compare different 2D feature extractors and axiomatic 3D descriptors and evaluate other components of our optimization module. As another validation, we show that the features generalize strongly to other tasks and get state-of-the-art results in part segmentation transfer.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Foundation models are finding their way into a growing number of downstream applications. They show strong generalization to tasks they were not explicitly trained for and exhibit surprising zero- or few-shot capabilities. Successful approaches have been presented for processing text or 2D images [1,2,3], but no prominent 3D methods aimed at local details are available yet. The main reasons are the diversity of 3D representations (i.e., meshes, point clouds, volumetric or implicit representations) and the comparably low availability of high-quality 3D data.

Recent works using 2D foundation models for shape analysis, like [4,5,6], have focused mainly on global tasks such as shape classification, or on segmentation, which represents a middle ground between global and local analyses [7]. This paper builds on this continuum, advancing from classification to segmentation and now to keypoints, with each stage requiring a more localized understanding of geometric details.

In this work, we focus on few-shot keypoint detection on 3D meshes. Repeatable keypoints enable a wide range of downstream applications, including rigid and non-rigid shape matching, object tracking, shape reconstruction, and shape manipulation [8,9,10,11,12], to name a few. Moreover, because keypoint detection requires both semantic and geometric shape understanding, it has been used in the past as a fruitful testbed for exploiting and evaluating various local shape descriptors [13,14] as well as consistency relations between 3D shapes and their views [15].

A natural approach to keypoint detection is to leverage dense 3D geometric features or descriptors, which ideally capture both global (semantic) and local (geometric) information at the same time. Previous works in this domain either focus on axiomatic features or pre-train models on 3D datasets [16,17]. Such methods, however, are limited by robustness issues and by the lack of diversity and amount of 3D training data, so existing approaches tend to have limited accuracy on complex 3D models. In contrast, we propose to retrieve informative features from powerful pre-trained 2D vision encoders, which can be used directly without any further training.

We show, for the first time, that such back-projected features enable a localized understanding of shape geometry while also capturing rich global semantic information. In particular, we demonstrate that these features are robust against rotations and scaling changes and can be computed for any point on the shape's surface and with any texture type. By assembling information from multiple rendered views around the shape, we show that even coarse 2D features can lead to dense 3D descriptors that vary continuously on the surface.

In addition to the lack of informative features, a common challenge in keypoint detection is the presence of symmetries: a successful method should detect all keypoints across various symmetries (e.g., different legs of a table) while avoiding superfluous detections. To address this, we introduce a simple yet effective optimization strategy that leverages the back-projected features and ensures that the detected keypoints are distributed on the target shapes similarly to the given few-shot examples.

Our main contributions are (1) the formalization of feature back-projection, including Gaussian geodesic re-weighting to handle noisy point visibility information, (2) an analysis of back-projected features from different recent foundation models and their properties, and (3) an optimization module that aims to match the average observed distribution of keypoints on the target shape. Our method achieves state-of-the-art results on the KeypointNet benchmark, improving over the best competing method by over 93% IoU on average over all evaluation distances. In an extensive ablation study, we compare different 2D feature extractors and axiomatic 3D descriptors and evaluate further components of our optimization module. As additional validation, we demonstrate strong generalization of the features to other tasks, achieving state-of-the-art results in part segmentation transfer.
